title: Rational Agent
body:
**An agent perceives an environment and acts on it. A *rational* agent selects the action expected
to maximise its performance measure, given what it has perceived and what it knows.**

That sentence is the frame the entire course sits in, and every block is a different answer to
"how does it choose": search the consequences ([[Best-First Search]]), evaluate them
([[Expected Utility]]), learn from examples ([[Supervised Learning]]), or learn from
consequences ([[Reinforcement Learning]]).

## Four things to specify before you can call anything rational

| | Question |
|---|---|
| **Performance measure** | what counts as doing well, stated by the designer |
| **Environment** | what it is acting in |
| **Actuators** | what it can do |
| **Sensors** | what it can perceive |

**The performance measure is imposed from outside and it is the one that goes wrong.** Score a
vacuum agent on dirt collected and it learns to dump dirt back out and collect it again. The agent
is behaving rationally; the measure was written badly. Specify what you want the world to look
like, never the behaviour you imagine getting there. This is the same failure as a
[[Genetic Algorithm|fitness function]] that rewards the wrong thing, and the same again as reward
shaping in [[Reinforcement Learning]]. Three blocks of this course, one mistake.

## Rational is not omniscient

Rationality is about **expected** performance given available information, not about the outcome.
Crossing a road after looking both ways is rational even if a piano falls on you. Judging agents
by results rather than by decisions makes the concept useless, because it turns every unlucky
correct decision into a mistake.

Three distinctions that follow from that:

- **Rational ≠ perfect.** Perfection needs the future; rationality needs only good use of the
  present.
- **Rational ≠ optimal-in-hindsight.** [[Expected Utility]] is the formalisation of that gap.
- Information gathering is rational. Exploring, experimenting, and looking both ways all pay
  off in expectation, which is why exploration appears again in [[Q-Learning]].

## Environment types, and why they decide the algorithm

| Property | Easy case | Hard case |
|---|---|---|
| Observable | fully: sensors give the whole state | partially: you must remember and infer |
| Determinism | deterministic | stochastic, so plans need probabilities |
| Agents | single | multiple, and then it is [[Game Trees|adversarial]] |
| Episodic | each decision independent | sequential: this action changes what is possible later |
| Static | world waits for you | dynamic: thinking has a cost measured in the world |
| Discrete | finite states and actions | continuous |

Read the right-hand column as a list of reasons an algorithm stops working. Classical search
assumes the left column almost everywhere: fully observable, deterministic, single-agent,
sequential, static, discrete. Every later block relaxes one of those, and **which one it relaxes
is the best way to remember what each block is for**. Stochastic gives you utility theory,
multi-agent gives you [[Game Trees]], unknown-and-sequential gives you reinforcement learning.

The theoretical ceiling on all of it is [[Turing Machine]] and [[Undecidability]]: an agent is a
program, so nothing here escapes those limits, and [[NP-Complete]] is why even the decidable parts
get [[Heuristic|heuristics]] instead of exact answers.
